title: Grayslake Issues First Permit for $18 Billion Illinois Data Center Campus
excerpt: T5 Data Centres' Cornerstone project would bring up to 6.7 million square feet of data-center space to 472 acres along Peterson Road — and a lawsuit from neighbors who say they never got a real say.
body:
• The village of Grayslake, Illinois issued the first building permit for T5 Data Centres' Cornerstone campus, clearing an 800,000-square-foot first building along Peterson Road.
  • The development envisions about 6.7 million square feet of data-center space on up to 472 acres over seven to ten years, backed by as much as $18 billion in private investment.
  • Grayslake calls it potentially the largest economic investment in Lake County history, projecting $1.4 billion in property tax revenue over 20 years — with no local tax incentives or subsidies.
  • Opponents, including residents of a nearby 55-plus community, say they were not given a real chance to weigh in and have sued, alleging inadequate hearings and Open Meetings Act violations; the case heads to court in November.

The village of Grayslake, Illinois has granted the first building permit for what could become the largest private development in Lake County history — an 800,000-square-foot data center that is the opening phase of T5 Data Centres' planned 472-acre campus along Peterson Road.

The scale of the build

The first building, part of T5's 'T5@Chicago IV' project, sits in the Cornerstone business park along Peterson Road west of Route 83. The latest plans call for about 6.7 million square feet of data-center space to be built over seven to ten years. Earlier approvals allowed for an even larger footprint of up to about 473 acres and as much as 10.1 million square feet, according to village documents.

Cost estimates vary. Grayslake Mayor Elizabeth Davies has described an $8.5 billion build, while T5 has said the figure could reach $12 billion to $18 billion. If fully built out, the campus would bring 1,500 permanent positions plus hundreds of construction and trade jobs during development, and the village said the initial permit marks the operational start of the campus, with site work moving forward.

The land was previously open farmland owned by the Alter family, which also owns the Chicago Sky women's professional basketball team. It sits in Grayslake's 'central range,' an area the village has long envisioned for development to diversify its property-tax base, with infrastructure such as a new water tower and an expanded Peterson Road already in place.

$1.4 billion in taxes — without subsidies

'Secured without local municipal tax incentives, tax exemptions or TIF (tax increment financing) subsidies, the development is projected to generate $1.4 billion in property tax revenue over 20 years across local taxing bodies,' the village said in announcing the permit.

Developer fees are still being negotiated but could reach the tens of millions if the project is fully built out. Davies said the village plans to use roughly 25 percent of the fees for resident cost-control measures such as reduced local fees, 25 percent for special community projects, and the remaining 50 percent for major infrastructure work.

Neighbors push back

Opposition has been persistent. Residents say they learned too late to weigh in before approvals were granted. Among the most organized are residents of Saddlebrook Farms, a 55-plus community of about 3,000 people near the site, who say no one from T5 ever held town halls or answered their questions directly.

Their concerns include 600 diesel backup generators, noise, the future of their well water, and upward pressure on ComEd electricity rates already hitting fixed incomes. Opponents have filed suit alleging, among other things, that the hearings were inadequate and Open Meetings Act rules were violated. The village has responded with a motion to dismiss, and the case is headed to court in November.

The dispute reflects a national pattern: communities across the country are pushing back against data-center proposals over power and water consumption, even as developers say demand for data-center capacity is 'off the charts.'

Diaspora angle

For the Indian diaspora in Chicago's suburbs, the campus is another marker of the AI infrastructure boom that is reshaping both American suburbs and the demand for the Indian IT talent that helps build, operate and service these facilities. Indian technology firms supplying data-center design, cloud migration and managed services stand directly in the path of this buildout.

What's next

Site work is moving forward on the first building. The immediate test is legal: November's court hearing will determine whether the opponents' claims about the approval process move ahead. Longer term, the questions that matter are whether power and water concerns reshape the project's later phases, and whether Grayslake's gamble — massive tax revenue in exchange for hosting the region's AI-era industrial core — pays off.
